title: Using and evaluating legislative history
summary: Legislative history comprises materials associated with a statute’s development that may supply evidence of its meaning and purposes.
notes:
Identify the material’s author, institutional role, timing, connection to the provision, and consistency with the enacted text. Katzmann places conference and committee reports above informed bill-manager explanations and stray statements by uninvolved members. He treats these materials as interpretive evidence rather than independently enacted commands.

Gayle uses committee and conference explanations to resolve geographic ambiguity. The Murphy litigation demonstrates a limit imposed by the Supreme Court: an express report statement did not establish expert-fee recovery against its reading of text and the Spending Clause notice requirement. Critics emphasize manipulation, contradictory materials, and constitutional enactment procedures. Katzmann responds with Congress’s reliance on reports, internal incentives for accuracy, and the usefulness of context. A careful account must state which material supports which inference rather than citing legislative history as an undifferentiated source.
